11.3 The Classification Theorem of Finite Abelian Groups Recall that we can list all abelian groups of order 𝑝𝑛. Well in fact, this can be extended easily to list all finite and finitely generated abelian groups! Example 11.3.1. Here we list (up to isomorphism) all abelian groups of order 729 = 36. Theorem 11.3.2. (The Fundamental Theorem of finite abelian Groups) If 𝐺 is a nontrivial finite abelian group then 𝐺 is isomorphic to a direct product of cyclic groups of prime power order, 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝 𝑒𝑛 𝑛 , where the primes 𝑝𝑖 are not necessarily distinct, the 𝑒𝑖 are natural numbers, and 𝑝𝑒1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 = |𝐺|. Moreover, this decomposition is unique, up to reordering of the factors. Warning! There are several different (equivalent) ways of stating this theorem! Some books will use ⊕ instead of ×. Other versions use Proposition 11.2.1 to write the factors in a differ- ent way (so they are no longer prime powers), for example writing 𝐶54 × 𝐶52 × 𝐶32 × 𝐶3 × 𝐶2 as 𝐶54⋅32⋅2 × 𝐶52⋅3 = 𝐶11250 × 𝐶75. We also have the following for finitely generated abelian groups. Theorem 11.3.3. (The Fundamental Theorem of Finitely Generated Abelian Groups) If 𝐺 is a nontrivial finitely generated abelian group then 𝐺 is isomorphic to, ℤ 𝑒0 × 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝 𝑒𝑛 𝑛 , where the primes 𝑝𝑖 are not necessarily distinct and the 𝑒𝑖 are natural numbers. Moreover, this decomposition is unique, up to reordering of the factors. Definition 11.3.4. If 𝐺 is a nontrivial finitely generated abelian group and ℤ 𝑒0 × 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 is its factorisation, then the number 𝑒0 is called the rank of 𝐺. Example 11.3.5. Up to isomorphism, the abelian groups of order 12 = 2 2 ⋅ 3 are 𝐶22 × 𝐶3 and 𝐶2 × 𝐶2 × 𝐶3. 103

[Advanced handout: You are NOT required to read this, it is here just in case you are interested] Proofs of the classification of finite and finitely generated abelian groups In this section we prove Theorem 11.2.4 and give an outline of the proof of Theorem 0.1.2. These proofs involve material from the whole of the course, and they are rather intricate. This section does not form part of the course and is supplied here only for students who are particularly interested. Theorem 11.2.4 follows easily from the following lemma. Lemma 11.3.6. Let 𝑝 be a prime and let 𝐺 be a finite abelian group of order 𝑝𝑛. If 𝑎 ∈ 𝐺 has maximal order, then 𝐺 ≅ ⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾 for some 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺. Proof. Now 𝑜(𝑎) = 𝑝𝑚 for some 𝑚 ≤ 𝑛. We proceed by induction. If 𝑛 = 1 then 𝐺 is cyclic and the lemma holds. Now suppose 𝑛 ∈ ℕ and the lemma holds for all finite abelian group of order 𝑝𝑘 with 𝑘 < 𝑛. If 𝐺 is cyclic then there is nothing to prove, so assume this is not the case. Since 𝐺 ≠ ⟨𝑎⟩, we can find 𝑏 ∈ 𝐺 such that 𝑏 has minimal order in 𝐺 ∖ ⟨𝑎⟩. This means of course that if 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 and 𝑜(𝑔) < 𝑜(𝑏) then 𝑔 ∈ ⟨𝑎⟩. Claim 1: For all 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 we have 𝑔𝑝𝑚 = 𝑒. Proof. Now 𝑜(𝑔)∣𝑝𝑛, so 𝑜(𝑔) = 𝑝𝑖 with 𝑖 ≤ 𝑚 (since 𝑜(𝑎) is maximal and equal to 𝑝𝑚). Therefore, 𝑔𝑝 𝑚 = 𝑔𝑝𝑖⋅𝑝𝑚−𝑖 = (𝑔𝑝𝑖) 𝑝𝑚−𝑖 = 𝑒𝑝𝑚−𝑖 = 𝑒. Claim 2: ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ ⟨𝑏⟩ = ⟨𝑒⟩ and 𝑜(𝑏) = 𝑝. Proof. Now 𝑜(𝑏𝑝) < 𝑜(𝑏) so by minimality of 𝑜(𝑏) we have 𝑏𝑝 ∈ ⟨𝑎⟩. In particular, 𝑏𝑝 = 𝑎 𝑖 for some 𝑖. By Claim 1, 𝑒 = (𝑏𝑝)𝑝𝑚−1 = (𝑎𝑖) 𝑝𝑚−1 = 𝑎𝑖⋅𝑝𝑚−1. Since 𝑜(𝑎) = 𝑝𝑚 we know 𝑝𝑚∣𝑖 ⋅ 𝑝𝑚−1 and therefore 𝑖 = 𝑝𝑗 for some 𝑗 ∈ ℕ. Define 𝑐 ∶= 𝑎 −𝑗𝑏 and note that 𝑐 ∉ ⟨𝑎⟩ (since if it were, then 𝑏 ∈ ⟨𝑎⟩ which is absurd). Moreover, 𝑐𝑝 = 𝑎 −𝑗𝑝𝑏𝑝 = 𝑎−𝑖𝑏𝑝 = 𝑏−𝑝𝑏𝑝 = 𝑒. To summarise: 𝑜(𝑐) = 𝑝 and 𝑐 ∉ ⟨𝑎⟩. By Lagrange’s Theorem, we know that 𝑜(𝑏) is a power of 𝑝. Hence, by the minimality of 𝑜(𝑏), we must have that 𝑜(𝑏) = 𝑜(𝑐) = 𝑝. Now 𝑜(𝑏) = 𝑝, so ⟨𝑏⟩ is cyclic of prime order. In particular, any nontrivial element of ⟨𝑏⟩ generates ⟨𝑏⟩. Therefore ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ ⟨𝑏⟩ must equal ⟨𝑒⟩ or ⟨𝑏⟩. Since 𝑏 ∉ ⟨𝑎⟩, the latter is impossible. Hence ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ ⟨𝑏⟩ = ⟨𝑒⟩. Claim 3: In 𝐺 ∶= 𝐺/⟨𝑏⟩, the element 𝑎 ∶= 𝑎⟨𝑏⟩ has order 𝑝𝑚, and this order is maximal in 𝐺. Proof. Since every element in 𝐺 has order at most 𝑝𝑚, the same is true of 𝐺. Hence, we need only show that 𝑜(𝑎) = 𝑝𝑚. Let us assume, for a contradiction, that 𝑜(𝑎) < 𝑝𝑚. Then 𝑎𝑝𝑚−1 = 𝑒. Hence (𝑎⟨𝑏⟩)𝑝𝑚−1 = 𝑎𝑝𝑚−1⟨𝑏⟩ = 𝑎𝑝𝑚−1 = 𝑒 = ⟨𝑏⟩. 104

Thus, 𝑎𝑝𝑚−1 ∈ ⟨𝑏⟩ ∩ ⟨𝑎⟩, and this is trivial by Claim 2. Hence 𝑎𝑝𝑚−1 = 𝑒, which is absurd. Claim 4: 𝐺 = ⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾 for some 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺. Proof. This follows from the induction hypothesis, because |𝐺| = |𝐺|/|⟨𝑏⟩| = 𝑝𝑛−1. Claim 5: 𝐺 is the internal direct product 𝐺 = ⟨𝑎⟩𝐾. Proof. Now 𝐾 corresponds to a subgroup 𝐾 with ⟨𝑏⟩ ≤ 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺 and 𝐾 = 𝐾/⟨𝑏⟩. Since |⟨𝑏⟩| = 𝑝, we have |𝐾| = |𝐾|/𝑝. If 𝑔 ∈ ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾, then 𝑔 ∈ ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾. However, by Claim 4 we know that ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾 = ⟨𝑒⟩. Therefore ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾 ⊆ ⟨𝑏⟩. However, by Claim 2 this then implies that ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾 = ⟨𝑒⟩. Since 𝐺 is abelian, we therefore have that: ⟨𝑎⟩ ⊴ 𝐺 and 𝐾 ⊴ 𝐺 and ⟨𝑎⟩ ∩ 𝐾 = ⟨𝑒⟩. It remains simply to check that ⟨𝑎⟩𝐾 = 𝐺, which we can show by proving that |⟨𝑎⟩𝐾| = |𝐺|. Now |⟨𝑎⟩𝐾| = |⟨𝑎⟩| ⋅ |𝐾| = |⟨𝑎⟩|(𝑝|𝐾|) = 𝑝𝑚𝑝|𝐾|. By Claim 3 the latter equals |⟨𝑎⟩|𝑝|𝐾| = 𝑝|⟨𝑎⟩𝐾|. By Claim 4 the latter equals 𝑝|𝐺| = 𝑝𝑛 = |𝐺|. Claim 6: 𝐺 ≅ ⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾. Proof. This follows immediately from Theorem 11.1.3 and Claim 5. Proof of Theorem 11.2.4. We proceed by induction on 𝑛. If 𝑛 = 1 then 𝐺 is cyclic of order 𝑝 and there is nothing to prove. Suppose the theorem is true for all groups of order 𝑝𝑘, for all 𝑘 < 𝑛. If 𝐺 is cyclic then there is nothing to prove, so suppose this is not the case. Let 𝑎 ∈ 𝐺 have maximal order. Then by Lemma 0.1.6 we can write 𝐺 ≅ ⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾, where 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺. Now 𝑝𝑛 = |⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾| = |⟨𝑎⟩| ⋅ |𝐾|. Hence |𝐾| = 𝑝𝑟 and |⟨𝑎⟩| = 𝑝𝑠 for some 𝑟, 𝑠 with 𝑟 + 𝑠 = 𝑛. Note that, since ⟨𝑎⟩ is cyclic, we have, ⟨𝑎⟩ ≅ 𝐶𝑝𝑠. Since |𝐾| = 𝑝𝑟 < 𝑝𝑛, we can apply the induction hypothesis to deduce that there are natural numbers 𝑒2, … , 𝑒𝑡 such that, 𝐾 ≅ 𝐶𝑝𝑒2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑡 , where 𝑝𝑒2 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑡 = 𝑝𝑟, and this factorisation of 𝐾 is unique up to reordering of the factors. Setting 𝑒1 ∶= 𝑠 we therefore have, 𝐺 ≅ ⟨𝑎⟩ × 𝐾 ≅ 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 × 𝐶𝑝𝑒2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑡 , where 𝑝𝑒1 ⋅ (𝑝𝑒2 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑡) = 𝑝𝑠𝑝𝑟 = 𝑝𝑛. Finally, we must show the factorisation is unique. By Proposition 11.1.1, the order of the factors doesn’t matter, so we can without loss of generality assume that 𝑝𝑒2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ 𝑝𝑒𝑡. Since the order of 𝑎 was chosen to be maximal, we also have 𝑝𝑒1 ≥ 𝑝𝑒2. If we are given another factorisation 𝐺 ≅ 𝐶𝑞𝑓1 × 𝐶𝑞𝑓2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑞𝑓𝑟 with 𝑞 prime and 𝑞𝑓1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ 𝑞𝑓𝑟 then the largest order of any element in 𝐺 is clearly 𝑞𝑓1. Since 𝑎 has maximal order in 𝐺, it follows that 𝑜(𝑎) = 𝑞𝑓1 and therefore 𝑝𝑒1 = 𝑞𝑓1. Hence, 𝐾 ≅ 𝐺/⟨𝑎⟩ ≅ 𝐺/𝐶𝑝𝑒1 ≅ 𝐺/𝐶𝑞𝑓1 ≅ 𝐶𝑞𝑓2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑞𝑓𝑟 . By the induction hypothesis, the factorisation of 𝐾 as 𝐶𝑝𝑒2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑡 is unique. 105

Outline of proof of Theorem 0.1.2. (The proof of Theorem 0.1.3 is similar) Let 𝐺 be a nontrivial finite abelian group. • Let 𝑝1, 𝑝2, … , 𝑝𝑟 be the distinct prime divisors of |𝐺|, and let 𝑃𝑖 be the Sylow 𝑝𝑖- subgroup of 𝐺 for 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. • Because 𝐺 is abelian, every subgroup is normal. Therefore 𝑃𝑖 ⊴ 𝐺 for all 𝑖. • For 𝑠 ≤ 𝑟 let Π𝑠 = 𝑃1𝑃2 ⋯ 𝑃𝑠. Because each 𝑃𝑖 ⊴ 𝐺, we have that Π𝑠 is a group, and therefore a subgroup of 𝐺. Moreover, for all 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 we have 𝑔−1(Π𝑠)𝑔 is equal to 𝑔−1𝑃1𝑔𝑔−1𝑃2𝑔𝑔−1 ⋯ 𝑔𝑔−1𝑃𝑠𝑔 = Π𝑠. Hence Π𝑠 ⊴ 𝐺. • Let 𝑠 ≤ 𝑟. Now |𝑃𝑠| is a power of 𝑝𝑠, so by Lagrange every element in 𝑃𝑠 has order a power of 𝑝𝑠. On the other hand, every element in Π𝑠−1 has order a product of powers of 𝑝1, … , 𝑝𝑠−1. Hence Π𝑠−1 ∩ 𝑃𝑠 = ⟨𝑒⟩. • We have shown that Π𝑠−1 ∩ 𝑃𝑠 = ⟨𝑒⟩ and both Π𝑠−1 and 𝑃𝑠 are normal in 𝐺 and therefore also normal in Π𝑠. Hence Π𝑠 is the internal direct product of Π𝑠−1 and 𝑃𝑠. • Hence (using an induction argument) one can show that: Π𝑟 ≅ Π𝑟−1 × 𝑃𝑟 ≅ Π𝑟−2 × 𝑃𝑟−1 × 𝑃𝑟 ≅ ⋯ ≅ 𝑃1 × ⋯ × 𝑃𝑟. • Since |𝐺| = 𝑝1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑟 = |𝑃1 × ⋯ × 𝑃𝑟| we see that Π𝑟 = 𝐺. Hence 𝐺 is isomorphic to the direct product 𝑃1 × ⋯ × 𝑃𝑟. • Each group 𝑃𝑖 is a finite abelian group whose order is 𝑝𝑛𝑖 𝑖 , and so we can apply The- orem 11.2.4 to 𝑃𝑖 to uniquely decompose it into a direct product of cyclic groups, like so: 𝑃𝑖 = 𝐶 𝑝𝑒𝑖,1 𝑖 × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑖,2 𝑖 × ⋯ × 𝐶 𝑝𝑒𝑖,𝑡𝑖 𝑖 • The result then follows immediately. 106
